This is the page as it stood on 2 October 2026, before the quiz moved into a web page. The current page

NIETE · Islamabad · live since 6 September 2026

A quiz from the lesson just taught

A teacher records a lesson for coaching. The recording is read back, the objectives that lesson actually covered are listed, and eight questions are written about those — not about a syllabus. The teacher forwards one message to the class group; the students answer on WhatsApp; the teacher gets a report on what to reteach. Since 25 September a quiz can also be written from the lesson plan the teacher used that day, without a recording. This page is the whole thing: how it works, then what twenty-seven days of it produced.

How it works

The feature adds one question to a teacher's day and nothing else. Everything below is the production copy and the production artefacts — the strings are lifted from the bot's own catalogue, the objective list, question card, scorecard and PDF are files the system really produced for one Grade 5 English lesson in Islamabad.

  1. 1

    A teacher records a lesson — which they were doing anyway

    Teachers already record a lesson to get coaching feedback. Nothing new is asked of them. The recording is transcribed, and the transcript is read back to list the objectives the lesson actually covered — not what a syllabus says it should have.

    That distinction is the whole point. The quiz can only ask about things the children were actually taught, that morning, by that teacher.

    Read back from the recording

    1. Identify similarities between two poems about city and farm life.recall
    2. Identify differences between two poems about city and farm life.recall
    3. Use a Venn diagram to categorize similarities and differences between two poems.apply

    The three objectives read out of one real Grade 5 English lesson, with the level each was taught at.

  2. 2

    The teacher is offered a quiz, once, and can say no

    The offer arrives after the coaching report. Two buttons, no form. The first time a teacher ever sees it, a 1:43 film rides along explaining what a quiz is.

    A yes takes about a minute to write. The teacher never picks a topic, a difficulty or a question count — all of that comes from the lesson itself.

    3:42 pm
    ‹ NIETE Teaching Assistantonline

    Your Grade 5 English lesson, City and Farm Life Comparison, Monday. I can make a short 8-question quiz your students take on WhatsApp — it checks what they learnt, and you get a report on what to reteach. Want it? You can make one for any lesson anytime by sending /quiz.

    3:41 pm

    Yes, make it

    3:42 pm ✓✓

    Making it now — about a minute. The quiz will arrive here with the message to forward.

    3:42 pm
    Message

    The offer and the acceptance — every word is the production string — and the film that rides the first offer a teacher ever gets. Urdu cut, 1:43.

  3. 3

    Two messages come back: one to keep, one to forward

    The first is a three-page PDF for the teacher — what was taught, what each question checks and why, with the correct answers marked. It exists so the teacher can see the quiz before the class does.

    The second is written for children, in the quiz language, and carries the class link. The teacher forwards it to the class WhatsApp group. No child’s number is ever needed, and none is ever stored.

    3:43 pm
    ‹ NIETE Teaching Assistantonline
    PDFGrade 5 English — City and Farm.pdf3 pages · 412 kB

    📝 Your quiz: Grade 5 English, City and Farm Life Comparison — 8 questions. This PDF is for you: what you taught, what the quiz checks, and every question with its correct answer marked. The NEXT message is for your students — forward it to the class group.

    3:43 pm

    Forward THIS message to your students:

    3:43 pm

    📚 *Quiz time!* Your teacher has sent you a quiz on *City and Farm Life Comparison* — what we studied on Monday. Tap here to start: niete.rumi.link/q/H7JXLK It takes about 5 minutes. You will be asked your name and class first.

    3:43 pm
    Message

    The handoff. The link shown here is a stand-in; a real one is a six-character class code.

  4. 4

    Page one of what the teacher gets

    Not a summary of the quiz — the quiz itself, with the reasoning. Teachers who have this before the class sits down can see whether the questions match what they meant to teach, and can reteach before the results arrive rather than after.

    The real PDF sent for this lesson. Only the teacher’s name and the class link are masked.

  5. 5

    A child taps the link and gives a name and a class

    The link opens WhatsApp, not a website. There is no app, no login and no password — the child types a first name and a class, and starts.

    Everything after this happens in the chat, one message at a time, so it works on a shared family handset over a weak connection.

    3:52 pm
    ‹ NIETE Teaching Assistantonline

    Here we go — 8 questions. Take your time!

    3:52 pm
    Message

    What the child sees first. Eight questions from their own teacher’s lesson.

  6. 6

    One question is one message

    Where the question needs a picture — notation, a diagram, a table, a long set of options — the whole question is drawn as an image and the buttons are just A, B and C. Otherwise the options are the buttons themselves.

    The reply is immediate and specific to the option tapped: not “wrong”, but why that particular answer was tempting and what the text actually said.

    2:23 pm
    ‹ NIETE Teaching Assistantonline

    ‏سوال اوپر تصویر میں ہے۔ A، B یا C دبائیں۔

    2:23 pm

    B

    2:23 pm ✓✓

    ✅ بہت خوب! اس جملے میں 'دل شکستہ' کا مطلب 'دکھا ہوا دل' صاف ظاہر ہو رہا ہے، جیسے مشکیزہ اپنی خامی کی وجہ سے اداس تھا۔

    2:23 pm
    Message

    A real question card from an Urdu quiz, the letter the child tapped, and the reply that child’s own teacher’s lesson generated for that exact option.

  7. 7

    A scorecard, then two offers

    The card is an image, so it survives being forwarded to a parent. Under it, two questions in turn: send this to a friend, and — if the child declines that — watch another video and do another quiz.

    The second offer is the door into the Taleemabad video library. It is the only point in the whole flow where a child is invited to do something nobody assigned, and it turns out to matter more than we expected.

    4:00 pm
    ‹ NIETE Teaching Assistantonline

    Want to send this quiz to a friend? I’ll tell you how they did once they finish.

    3:59 pm

    No thanks

    4:00 pm ✓✓

    Want to watch more videos and take more quizzes?

    4:00 pm
    Message

    The two offers in the order a child meets them, and the card that comes before them — rendered by the production code with a real result; only the name is changed.

  8. 8

    The teacher gets a report — and a nudge if nobody came

    The class report goes out when everyone who started has finished, or twelve hours after the first child starts, whichever comes first. If more children finish later, a single follow-up goes out rather than a stream of them.

    And if almost nobody has started six hours on, the teacher gets exactly one reminder — never inside 21:00–07:00, never more than one a day, and if several of their quizzes are quiet they are named together in one message.

    9:44 pm
    ‹ NIETE Teaching Assistantonline

    You will get a report on how the class did about 12 hours after the first student starts — or sooner if everyone finishes. Send /quiz anytime to see your quizzes or fetch a report.

    3:43 pm

    1 student(s) have started your quiz on *City and Farm Life Comparison* so far. Worth forwarding the link to the class group again?

    9:44 pm
    Message

    The promise, and the one nudge. Both are capped deliberately — the reminders were annoying before they were.

How far it has reached

Since the first quiz went out on 6 September, 8,831 different children have sat at least one, sent by 1,684 different teachers. Both lines are still climbing every day. They are climbing more slowly than in the first week: the most children seen for the first time on one day was 638, on 9 September; 2 October brought 203, and new teachers per school day have gone from over a hundred to 38.

8,831children reached since launch
1,684teachers who sent at least one quiz
819children on an average day
4,613children who came back on more than one day — 52% of everyone

Where the children come from

Every teacher belongs to a school, and every ICT school to one of six sectors, so both the teachers and the children can be placed. Across the six, 22.7% of the 6,729 teachers on the roll have sent at least one quiz, from 321 of the 433 schools. Sihala leads on penetration (31.1% of its teachers); Urban-I carries the most children (3,907) because it is the biggest sector. Mastery barely moves between them — Urban-I at 75.6%, Urban-II at 70.7% — which is the point: the quiz is written from the lesson, and the lessons are the same curriculum everywhere.

Every day since launch

School days carry the feature; weekends run lower. What has changed is who turns up. In the first days almost every child was new. Since 12 September, returning children have outnumbered new ones on 21 of 21 days — the same children are coming back, and they bring the day's activity with them.

How fast it is growing

A child counts as new on the day of their first quiz ever; a teacher on the day they first receive a quiz with a class link. Since the launch, 8,620 children and 1,643 teachers have arrived that way. (Another 286 children and 49 teachers had used the ready-made video quizzes before 6 September and are not counted as new.)

With the week of 28 Sep complete: 1,722 new children in the week of 21 Sep, 1,600 in the week of 28 Sep (-7%); 340 new teachers, then 308 (-9%). 1 Oct falls inside the week of 28 Sep and was undercounted: WhatsApp did not deliver the bot's messages for part of that afternoon. On a bigger base the totals grow more slowly in percentage terms: about 4% more children a school day in the week of 28 Sep, against 50% and more in the first days.

One day stands out. On 25 Sep, 120 teachers received their first quiz — the most since 10 Sep — and 79 of them came through the lesson-plan offer that went out that afternoon. New children did not jump the same day (388, 91 of them from a lesson-plan quiz): the classes of those teachers had one evening, and then a weekend.

The weekend of 26–27 Sep

Saturday and Sunday are not school days, so a weekend is set against the other weekends, not against the week. Over 26–27 Sep 1,168 children sat a quiz (792 on Saturday, 481 on Sunday), 2,819 sittings in all, and 458 children took their first quiz ever. That is the biggest weekend so far on all three counts; the weekend before had 947 children, 2,183 sittings and 349 new children. The lesson-plan quizzes from Friday afternoon made the difference: 413 children sat one over the weekend (783 sittings), while sittings on coaching quizzes were lower than the weekend before (1,234 against 1,744). New teachers are few on any weekend, because teachers send quizzes on school days: 21 this time (19 on Saturday, 14 of them by a lesson-plan quiz), against 6, 9 on the earlier weekends. The AI-coaching route

The quiz began as the last step of AI coaching: a teacher records a lesson, gets the coaching report, and is offered a quiz written from that recording. Since the launch 1,389 teachers have received a quiz this way and 7,544 children have sat one; 6,724 of those children finished at least one. For 1,332 of the teachers and 7,065 of the children, a coaching quiz was their first quiz of any kind — 81% of every new teacher and 82% of every new child since the launch.

An offer is made after every coaching report, so one teacher can be offered many times; 2,312 offers were turned down and the rest went unanswered. The child counts here are children on the coaching quizzes themselves, not the library quizzes they chose afterwards. On the evening of 29 Sep, from 21:25 until 01:11, the AI service the bot uses was unavailable, so coaching reports and quizzes asked for in those hours failed; the counts here are a little lower for it. The table follows quizzes that began as an offer; a teacher can also make a coaching quiz straight from the /quiz menu, and the children on those account for the difference from the 7,544 above.

Is the interest real?

On 25 Sep a second way in opened for every teacher. At 15:00, teachers who had used a lesson plan that day are offered a quiz on that lesson, with no recording needed. The offer has now run on six afternoons: Fri 25 Sep (606 teachers), Mon 28 Sep (520 teachers), Tue 29 Sep (410 teachers), Wed 30 Sep (622 teachers), Thu 1 Oct (563 teachers), Fri 2 Oct (428 teachers). 2,087 different teachers have been offered at least once and 680 of them on more than one afternoon; 389 have said yes at least once. From 28 Sep a short intro film for teachers went with all of the offers on the first afternoon it ran and with part of them after that (the table shows how many).

Thu 1 Oct is not comparable. From 13:45 to 15:27 Pakistan time that day WhatsApp did not deliver the bot's messages, about 1 hour 41 minutes in all. The 15:00 offer went out inside that window (563 offers between 15:04 and 15:17), so almost none arrived, and 0 teachers said yes. Children who opened a quiz in the window got no questions. Its column is shown for completeness and is left out of every rate and every "typical afternoon" line below.

Below, every afternoon side by side, all counted to the end of Fri 2 Oct. The newest cohorts are only hours old: the 2 Oct offers had about 9 hours before the count stopped and the 1 Oct ones a day and 9 hours, against 7 days for 25 Sep. A late yes still counts for the afternoon it answers. On the evening of 29 Sep the AI service the bot uses was unavailable from 21:25 until 01:11 the next morning, so quizzes and coaching reports asked for in those hours failed: 6 lesson-plan quizzes could not be written that evening.

A coaching offer is made after every coaching report, at any hour, so it is the day's yardstick rather than a like-for-like match. Class reports go out from the next morning, so the newest afternoons have few or none yet. The lesson-plan columns count only quizzes made from each afternoon's offer; teachers also made lesson-plan quizzes themselves from the /quiz menu on those days (14 on 25 Sep, 31 on 28 Sep, 31 on 29 Sep, 23 on 30 Sep, 14 on 1 Oct, 16 on 2 Oct).

When the first child arrived

A quiz made at 15:00 has one evening before midnight, so the fair line is "a child by midnight", set against coaching quizzes whose class link went out after 15:00 on the earlier weeks' same weekday. Over the five comparable afternoons, 106 of 381 lesson-plan quizzes had a child by that midnight (28%), against 164 of 481 (34%) for the after-15:00 coaching yardstick and 335 of 583 (57%) for every coaching quiz made on the same days.

What the numbers show, plainly (the five comparable afternoons only):

  • About one teacher in six says yes. 463 of 2,586 offers (18%) so far, 420 of them on the day (20%, 13%, 18%, 16%, 14% on the day, afternoon by afternoon). Coaching offers, across every one since the launch, get a yes 26% of the time. Most teachers do not answer at all; few say no (167 in all).
  • The reach is what makes it big. One afternoon's send reaches 410–622 teachers and makes 54–122 quizzes; a whole day of coaching offers reaches 281–584 teachers (the send reached more on four of the five afternoons). How many can be asked moves with the calendar: after the weekend, 258 teachers who had used a lesson plan on 28 Sep were outside WhatsApp's one-day window, against 39, 25, 32, 19 on the other afternoons.
  • Fewer lesson-plan quizzes reach a class. By midnight 28%, against 34% for coaching links sent after 15:00 ; the late hour explains part of the gap with coaching quizzes in general, not all of it. The 25 Sep quizzes, with the longest run, stand at 42 of 111 (38%) by the end of 2 Oct.
  • Once a quiz reaches a class, the class behaves the same. 9.4 children per lesson-plan quiz that reached anyone and 8.6 per coaching quiz made the same days; 82% and 86% of those children finished.
  • The film is not a result. The afternoons differ in more than the film: the weekday, the mix of teachers (680 have been offered more than once), and how long each has had to run. Nothing here isolates the film, so no difference between the afternoons is put down to it.
So far: six afternoons, five of them comparable (1 Oct went out while messages were not being delivered), and the newest only hours old. One lesson-plan send reaches about as many teachers as a whole day of coaching offers; about 18% say yes, against 26% for coaching. Fewer of their quizzes reach a class by midnight (28% against 34% for coaching links sent after 15:00). Still no verdict, and nothing here says what the film did; more school days with the offer running will say more.

Which way they came in

There are now three ways a quiz reaches a class: after AI coaching (written from the recorded lesson), after a lesson plan (written from the plan the teacher used that day — in the /quiz menu since the night of 24 September, and offered to every teacher at 15:00 on 25, 28, 29 and 30 September and 1 and 2 October), and a ready-made video quiz the teacher picks from the library. Children also reach the library on their own after a scorecard; that is counted separately, because no teacher sent it.

1,389teachers by AI coaching · 7,544 children
430teachers by lesson plan · 1,606 children, all since 25 Sep
115teachers sent a ready-made video quiz · 1,334 children
1,672children who chose a library quiz themselves

On 25 Sep the lesson-plan route was already the larger of the two for teachers — 124 teachers against 95 by coaching, 244 in all. For children it was smaller (241 against 671), because coaching quizzes from earlier in the week were still being sat and the lesson-plan quizzes had one evening. Over the weekend that followed, the lesson-plan quizzes went on being sat: 413 children sat one on 26–27 Sep against 636 on coaching quizzes, while only 51 teachers sent any quiz at all. On 2 Oct, the sixth offer afternoon, 63 teachers received a lesson-plan quiz and 66 a coaching one (144 in all); 226 children sat a lesson-plan quiz and 419 a coaching one.

The overlap is small. Of the 430 teachers who have had a lesson-plan quiz, 165 have also had a coaching quiz at some point; 263 have only the lesson-plan one, and 267 had never received any quiz before. The 15:00 offer skips anyone coached that day, so a teacher rarely gets both on one day (11 times since the launch). Of the 1,606 children on lesson-plan quizzes, 855 have also sat a coaching quiz and 815 were new. Grades 6–12 joined the lesson-plan route on 28 Sep: 10 quizzes so far from 6 teachers, all made from the /quiz menu rather than the 15:00 offer, sat by 37 children. They are counted in the lesson-plan figures above.

Someone who used two routes on one day is counted in both columns and once under "Any". Totals since the launch: 1,684 teachers and 8,831 children across all routes.

Where it lands

Two funnels, because two different things are being counted. A quiz is offered to one teacher; a quiz that is sent reaches a whole class. The wall is neither authoring nor delivery — it is a teacher deciding, on a given afternoon, that this lesson is worth a quiz.

Past that wall the chain holds: 93% of accepted quizzes are written and sent, and 1845 of them have been opened by at least one child. What happens to those children is the rest of this page.

Did they get it?

74.2%

of the objectives they were asked about, children mastered — every question on that objective right. 105,043 child-and-objective pairs, from 23,939 finished quizzes.

It was 78.7% after the first hundred children, 77.9% after nine hundred, and 75.9% at four days. Twenty-seven days and 23,939 finished quizzes in, it is 74.2% — still drifting down, a point or so at a time, the direction you expect as a sample stops being the keenest families and starts being everyone. Question by question the figure is higher — 82.8% of answers were right, the median child scored 88% — but the stricter reading is the useful one: a child who misses one of the two questions on fractions as parts of a whole has not mastered it, however good the score looks.

Where the questions get hard

Every question is written at a level — remembering, understanding, or applying. Apply questions cost every year something, and only a little: the gap between the easiest level and the hardest is 5 points, not the six it looked like on day one.

By grade — the grade each child typed when joining — the spread across every year with real numbers behind it is 10.2 points. On day one grade 3 looked eight points behind grade 4; that was small-sample noise and the page said so when it washed out. Urdu quizzes came back 4 points above English ones, and that gap has held every day since.

What was assessed, and how each grade did on it

Every quiz is written from what one teacher taught in one lesson, so the objectives are the teachers' own — 7,758 of them, across 1389 topics and 1807 quizzes that reached a child. The grade here is the one the lesson was taught at, which is where the objective belongs; the table above uses the grade the child typed. Each cell is the share of child-and-objective pairs mastered, with the number of pairs beneath it; cells with fewer than 30 are left blank.

What they did next

The quiz the teacher sent turned out to be the beginning, not the end.

When a child finishes, the assistant asks whether they want another. Nobody expected much of that offer. Of the 10859 children who saw it and answered, 5913 said yes — 54%. And the offer is the smaller half of it: children also came back on their own, through links their teacher had sent days before — re-opening a quiz long after the lesson it came from.

6447quizzes children chose for themselves, beyond the one their teacher sent
4203of those finished to the last question — 65%, against 67% on the quizzes teachers sent; a library quiz is roughly twice as long
3340children did three or more different quizzes in twenty-seven days
55the deepest run — 55 different quizzes across seven subjects

This counts different quizzes. Children also restarted quizzes they had already begun — 18,798 times across twenty-seven days — which is a separate story, part enthusiasm and part a rate-limit stall that has since been fixed. It is left out of every number above so that "went deeper" never means "tapped the same link twice".

The same quiz again

2,779 children have finished a quiz and then sat that same quiz again — 31% of everyone reached, across 7,456 repeat sittings. It happens every day, weekends included. The class report and the class card count each child once, using their latest attempt, so a child who repeats a quiz to improve is ranked on the result they ended with.

Library or friend?

After the scorecard a child is offered two things: more quizzes from the video library, or sending this quiz to a friend. More children say yes to the friend — 3,072 have tapped it, against 2,772 who went into the library. But the library is where children actually end up. Only 170 friends have arrived through an invite, so for every friend who joins, around 16 children have gone on to a library quiz themselves.

What a child receives

When the teacher's report goes out, every child who finished gets a class card: their score, the class average, and where they stand among the top of the class. A child who finishes after the report gets theirs straight away. These are three cards from real classes, drawn by the production renderer from the real scores. The names are invented; nothing else is changed.

One child, two evenings

A grade-4 child in Islamabad. The name is not Zara; everything else here is exactly as it happened, from the timestamps to the scores. Their teacher sent one quiz on Monday afternoon — Urdu grammar, from that morning's lesson.

Tap any quiz below to replay it. You will see what Zara saw, in order — every question exactly as it reached the phone, what was tapped, and what came back — and, for the second child further down, the video that arrived first. Green is right, red is wrong.

    Read it downwards. Zara did the Urdu grammar quiz, scored 88%, and forty minutes later did it again for 100%. A fractions quiz was opened that evening and put down. On Tuesday a second Urdu quiz turned up — synonyms — the first two questions fumbled, then a restart and everything right; then again; then, hours later, once more. In between came two English poems about the city and the farm for a grade-5 quiz, and the day ended on Three States of Matter.

    Five different quizzes. Four subjects. Fifty-five of fifty-eight answers right. Nobody sent the last four.

    The child who watched the videos

    Zara's quizzes came from a teacher's recording, so there was no video to watch. Many children take the other road: after a quiz they are offered the Taleemabad video library, and a quiz follows each film. This is one of them — a grade-2 child, call them Bilal, on Tuesday afternoon. Four videos across three subjects in two hours: repeated subtraction, Urdu nouns, when to use a and an, then place value. Each replay below starts with the actual video Bilal received, whole, with its caption exactly as sent — then the questions that followed it. Where a question had narration, the clip that played is there too.

      Bilal answered 47 questions that afternoon and got 37 right. The library quizzes are adaptive — longer than the eight-question transcript quizzes, and they get harder as a child gets things right — which is why these run to fifteen questions.

      Left to themselves, what do they pick?

      Of the 6447 quizzes children chose on their own, maths now leads, then English and Urdu — English led on day two and maths has overtaken it since. They do not stay in their lesson, and they do not stay in their year: 472 sittings were on grade 6–8 material, 1031 on grades 1–2. They reach up and down.

      Send it to a friend

      After the scorecard, one question: Want to send this quiz to a friend? I'll tell you how they did once they finish. Over twenty-seven days, 29,343 children saw it and 5812 tapped yes — 20%. Children want to send it. What we cannot yet show is anyone arriving.

      This is the one number on this page that was wrong, and it is worth saying plainly. An earlier version of this page reported friends arriving in the hundreds. They did not. Of the 2722 sittings the database records as arriving through an invite, 2407 name the joining child as their own inviter — a child re-opened the link they had just minted, and the join matched them back to their own record. Strip those and the honest figure is 315 sittings from 170 children, each with a different name and a different handset from whoever invited them; 178 finished. The offer works. The loop, so far, does not.

      This is the message that goes back. It is the production string with real numbers from one pair of children; the names are changed.

      🎯 Hamza finished your quiz!

      Hamza: 7/8
      You: 5/8

      Hamza edged you this time — worth another go.

      8:14 pm

      Adverbs of Manner, Time, Place, and Frequency — the friend edged the inviter.

      🎯 Areeba finished your quiz!

      Areeba: 7/8
      You: 7/8

      A dead heat — you both got the same.

      8:14 pm

      Vocabulary related to emotions and change — a dead heat. 14 of the 40 genuine pairs where both children finished the same quiz tied.

      One thing to fix. That message is English regardless of the quiz's language — an Urdu-speaking child who sends an Urdu quiz to a friend hears back in English. It bypasses the string catalogue. Small, and worth doing.

      How much weight this carries

      • Twenty-seven days, 23,939 finished quizzes, 8,831 children. The headline ran 78.8% → 77.9% → 75.9% → 74.2% as the sample grew from a hundred children to 8,831; the cuts beneath it are less settled, and one of them already washed out.
      • The children are self-selected. They are the ones whose parents opened a WhatsApp link. 1830 of 3667 quizzes ever reached a child — the biggest loss in the whole chain, and it sits after everything that has been fixed.
      • Nobody was watching them answer. A quiz done at home can be done with help — which is also, sometimes, the point.
      • Depth counts different quizzes only. The 18,798 restarts are excluded throughout.
      • Zara is a real child; the name is not. No child's name, class or number appears on this page.
